Willow ptarmigan chicks emerge from eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], with hatching occurring after approximately 21 days [ab = approximately 21 days], a developmental period consistent with that of other arctic-breeding galliforms. At the moment of hatching, these precocial neonates typically weigh around 8.8 grams [Wwb = around 8.8 grams], a value reflecting the modest energetic reserves contained within the calcareous egg. This relatively small initial mass demands that the downy chick begin foraging almost immediately under the vigilant guidance of its parents. The rapid transition from yolk dependence to exogenous feeding is critical in the short subarctic summer, where insects and tender plant shoots are abundant but only briefly available. Following hatching, the young birds exhibit coordinated mobility within hours, a trait that aids in thermoregulation and predator evasion across the open tundra landscape. Brooding by the hen remains essential during cold spells, but the chick's own capacity for endothermy develops steadily over the first several days of life.

By approximately twelve days after hatching [tx = approximately twelve days after hatching], the developing chick reaches the fledging stage, marked by the emergence of pin feathers and the ability to make short, fluttering flights. This fledging age is notably rapid for a bird of its size, an adaptation that minimizes the window of vulnerability to mammalian predators such as arctic foxes. The feather-growing nestling transitions quickly from a diet dominated by invertebrates to one increasingly composed of willow buds and leaves, reflecting the seasonal phenology of its habitat. Once the fledgling can sustain brief powered flight, it begins to accompany the parents on foraging excursions, learning to identify nutritious plant patches while still receiving some parental provisioning. This stage represents a critical threshold in the juvenile's development, as the energetic demands of feather synthesis and locomotion escalate sharply. The ultimate wet weight of adult ptarmigan, typically around 596 grams [Wwi = around 596 grams], is attained through a sustained growth trajectory that extends well beyond the fledging period, requiring several months of dedicated feeding.

Sexual maturation in the willow ptarmigan proceeds on a relatively compressed schedule given the brevity of the arctic breeding season. Male chicks begin to show the first signs of gonadal development and the acquisition of breeding plumage around 36 days after hatching [tp = around 36 days after hatching], a remarkably early onset of puberty for a galliform species of this body mass. This early reproductive activation is likely driven by the selective pressure to secure a territory and attract a mate during the brief window of snowmelt when resources are most plentiful. Females lag slightly behind males in the maturation of their reproductive organs, but both sexes exhibit this accelerated timeline compared to temperate relatives. The early attainment of sexual maturity is further corroborated by field observations of subadult birds engaging in courtship displays and pairing behaviors during their first summer. This strategy carries inherent risks, as young breeders may lack the experience to optimize nest placement or the body condition to withstand prolonged incubation fasts, but the potential payoff in terms of lifetime fitness is substantial in a short-lived species.

The time since birth at first brood is approximately one year, or 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], meaning that most individuals hatched in June will participate in nesting activities the following spring. This pattern of first reproduction at one year of age is common among arctic-nesting birds that face a severe constraint on the number of breeding attempts possible over a lifetime. Females typically lay a single clutch per season, and the maximum reproductive rate is achieved when a pair successfully produces 6 eggs per year [Ri = 6 eggs per year], a modest output compared to many temperate phasianids. The incubation period is demanding, requiring the hen to remain on the nest almost continuously for the 21-day duration at 34 °C [T = 34 °C], with the male providing vigilant territorial defense during this time. Predation and weather-related nest failure are common, so even this maximum reproductive output only marginally offsets annual mortality rates.

Longevity records for wild willow ptarmigan indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years], an unexpectedly short duration for a bird of its size that likely reflects the extreme physiological demands of life in a high-latitude environment. The combined stresses of harsh winters, nutritional bottlenecks, and high predation pressure truncate the potential lifespan relative to more southerly galliforms of comparable mass. Senescence becomes apparent in older birds through decreased feather quality, diminished foraging efficiency, and reduced reproductive output in females. The trade-off between early reproduction and somatic maintenance is stark in this species, as individuals that invest heavily in breeding during their first year may suffer reduced survival probabilities in subsequent winters. Despite this apparent constraint, the population persists through high fecundity in favorable years and a degree of nomadism that allows birds to track local peaks in food abundance. The interplay between the observed adult body mass of approximately 596 grams [Wwi = approximately 596 grams] and this brief projected lifespan of 9 years [am = 9 years] underscores the fast-paced life-history strategy that characterizes this arctic specialist.
